subject: Evaluation workplan & SLA comparison — next tests and incident expectations
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
To: Sylvia Klein <sylvia.klein@avahealth.com>
Cc: Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwood.ai>, Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.ai>
Date: Sun, 07 Mar 2026 15:12:00 -0700
Subject: Evaluation workplan & SLA comparison — next tests and incident expectations

Hi Sylvia — thanks again for a productive demo earlier. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we can keep momentum on the evaluation vs Vertex/other providers and lock down expectations for incident response.

Recap of what we covered
- Key priorities: P99 latency for interactive features (<= 200ms target for 512-token context) and predictable per-token cost for high-volume batch inference.
- Current evaluation scope at Ava Health: latency-sensitive triage assistant + nightly bulk embeddings for search re-rank.
- You flagged two competitive concerns: (1) how our support & RCA cadence compares to hyperscalers, and (2) how automatic failover / model fallbacks behave during incidents.

Proposed evaluation workplan (short & concrete)
1) Latency / cold-start test (1 day): 1000 short requests at target concurrency (simulate interactive usage). Owner: Redwood SE (Sean) — target week of Mar 16.
2) Throughput stress & degradation (2 days): sustained 1M tokens/hour for 48 hours to validate cost profile and autoscaling behavior. Owner: Ava engineering + Redwood ops.
3) Incident simulation (1 day): controlled fault injection (node kill / network partition) to observe fallback, routing, and KV cache behavior; validate logging and traces for RCA. Owner: Joint.

What we’ll deliver
- A one-page test matrix (attached: redwood-eval-matrix.xlsx) with inputs, success criteria, and data collection hooks.
- SLA/incident comparison (attached: sla-comparison.pdf) summarizing P99/P95 targets, escalation paths, and RCA timelines vs typical hyperscaler behavior.
- A sample escalation flow diagram (we’ll provide the PNG during the incident sim).

Open questions for you (please confirm by EOD Tue)
- Desired business hours for a phone-based escalation point (we can provide 24/7 for Dedicated customers; for hosted plans we provide email+chat with configurable paging).
- Any constraints for running the throughput test in your environment (IP allowlist, PO/contract needed, or preferred test AWS region)?

Next steps / asks
- If agreeable I’ll loop in our legal/procurement contact and schedule the latency test for Mar 16.
- Please confirm procurement contact for PO / NDA (cc’d: procurement@avahealth.com if that’s the right address).

Attachments: redwood-eval-matrix.xlsx (Excel), sla-comparison.pdf (PDF)

Thanks — looking forward to running the tests.

—
Marissa Cole
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
marissa.cole@redwood.ai | +1 (415) 555-0123

Hi Marissa,

Thanks for the clear recap — very helpful. A couple quick clarifications before we lock dates:

1) SLA / RCA expectations: your doc is a good start but we need to understand the worst-case timelines. For comparisons, our procurement team is seeing vendor RCAs that take 5–10 business days to produce a final RCA for Sev1 incidents from AWS/GCP, with an interim blameless summary within 72 hours. Can you confirm what Redwood commits to for hosted vs Dedicated?

2) Escalation contact: procurement@avahealth.com is correct for PO routing. For technical escalation we’d like a named contact and phone number for Sev1 during the test window.

3) Tests: the latency/cold-start test scope looks fine. For the throughput run — can it be run from an IP range we control (we prefer the test traffic originate from our VPC)? Also we’ll need a short statement of liability for the simulated fault window (our legal will request it).

We’re also running a parallel evaluation of Vertex AI (for model hosting) and a smaller internal inference stack. Key decision criteria: predictable cost at scale, RCA cadence, and observable traces for compliance audits.

If you can answer the SLA/RCA question and give a proposed named escalation contact I’ll get procurement to queue the PO and schedule the test week.

Best,
Sylvia Klein
CTO, Ava Health
sylvia.klein@avahealth.com

Subject: Re: Evaluation workplan & SLA comparison — next tests and incident expectations

Hi Sylvia — Sean on the SE side. Quick answers to the SLA/RCA questions and a technical sketch for the incident sim.

Summary of Redwood commitments (Hosted vs Dedicated)
- Hosted API (standard): Operational support via email/chat (business hours). P95/P99 telemetry available in console. Escalation to on-call engineer if the issue meets our Sev1 criteria. Initial incident acknowledgement within 1 hour during business hours; interim update within 8 hours. Final RCA typically delivered in 7–10 business days for complex system-level incidents.
- Dedicated (reserved capacity): 24/7 phone + pager, 15 minute acknowledgement target for Sev1, interim update within 2 hours, final RCA target: 5 business days for the initial RCA, with a follow-up writeup if deeper root cause work is required (no longer than 10 business days).

How this compares to hyperscalers (high level)
- Hyperscaler typical: broad SLAs for infrastructure; vendor RCAs often follow internal change windows and can be slower (5–10 business days, sometimes longer for multi-region incidents). They provide deep infrastructure telemetry but fewer application-level fallbacks tuned for LLM serving (relying on customer-managed retries and multi-region routing).
- Redwood differentiator: automatic model variant fallback + routing policy that can downgrade to a quantized/cheaper variant in-place to preserve availability while keeping latency bounded; built-in KV cache reuse across instances reduces cold-start impact. Also we provide a customer-visible incident timeline stream (correlated traces + per-request ids) to simplify audits.

RCA & Evidence we provide
- Initial blameless summary: within 48 hours for Dedicated, within 72–96 hours for Hosted (documented interim timeline and containment actions).
- Final RCA: objective timeline above. We include: sequence of events, traces (sampled request ids), kernel/runtime metrics, operator actions, mitigation steps, and recommended config changes.

Incident simulation plan (technical)
- Controlled node kill during sustained throughput: observe routing fallback, autoscaler response, and per-request tracing.
- Network partition simulation (short window): validate degraded routing and cache behavior.
- Data collection: we’ll stream logs and traces to a temporary secure bucket (you can decide if you want a copy).

Attachments: incident-escalation-flow.png (illustrates the on-call + customer paging flow)

Named escalation contact (for test window)
- Primary: Sean Gallagher, Redwood SE — +1 (415) 555-0189, sean.gallagher@redwood.ai (available during the lab/test window).

If that works we can schedule the latency run on Mar 16 and the throughput + incident sim on Mar 17–18 (contingent on PO/NDA). I’ll prepare a short test-run checklist and share it by Wed.

—
Sean Gallagher
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
